title: Infra GPU Capacity, Cloud Accounts & IaC CI/CD Playbook
author: Michael Chen
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's operational standards and runbooks for GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC module usage, CI/CD build & deploy pipelines, and common infra runbooks. It's intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate and evolve Redwood's inference fleet and control plane.

Scope: covers hosted and dedicated deployment surfaces, AWS (primary), GCP (secondary), and on-prem reference patterns. It does NOT replace security-compliance-specific runbooks (see security-and-compliance space).

Owner & Contacts
- Document owner: engineering (Infra team)
- Primary oncall: infra-sre rotation (see oncall schedule)
- Slack channels: #infra, #gpu-ops, #deployments
- Pager escalation: infra-sre -> infra-eng -> eng-vp per incident severity

Quick links
- Terraform modules: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac
- GPU runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026.json
- CI/CD templates: /confluence/eng-infra/team-wiki/infra-ci-cd-and-gpu-build-pipeline-2026.json

Principles
- Predictable performance: capacity planning targets 99th percentile latency SLOs for inference endpoints.
- Infrastructure as code: all changes to production infra must be made via tracked Terraform modules and reviewed PRs.
- Small, safe deployments: use canaries and automated rollback for model-serving changes.
- Observable by default: every service must export the metrics listed below and ship logs to the centralized observability stack.

Architecture overview
- GPU fleet: managed as an autoscaling pool of instance groups per region/instance-class. Each group runs the Redwood serving runtime on a GPU-optimized AMI/container image.
- Control plane: Kubernetes-based control plane for orchestration, runs on reserved CPU-only nodes; inference containers run on GPU nodes using node selectors and device plugins.
- Networking: centralized VPC per account with segmented subnets for control plane, inference, and management traffic. Transit Gateway (AWS) connects customer VPCs in dedicated deployments.

SLOs & Key metrics (summary)
| Metric | Target | Alert threshold | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Inference 99th p50 token latency (per model class) | <= 250 ms | >= 350 ms for 5m | infra-sre / serving-runtime |
| Pod restart rate (per node group) | < 1% / hour | >= 3% / 15m | infra-sre |
| GPU utilization (avg over 5m) | 50-80% | > 85% (sustained 10m) | infra-eng |
| Queue length (pending requests) | < 20 requests per instance | >= 50 for 2m | infra-sre |

Capacity planning: GPU fleet
- Baseline sizing: plan for peak qPS and tokens/sec with 1.5x headroom to account for traffic bursts and degraded performance.
- Safety buffer: maintain at least 10% spare capacity (unallocated GPUs) per region to enable fast scale and drain windows during rollouts.
- Predictive autoscaling: use mixed signals (queue length, avg latency, GPU utilization) to scale up. Scale down only after sustained low utilization for 15 minutes.
- Model placement: label node pools by instance type and quantization profile (e.g., p4d-quantized, a100-fp16). Prefer colocating frequently co-invoked models to improve KV cache locality.

Example capacity worksheet (excerpt)
| Region | Instance class | GPUs | Target qPS | Baseline nodes | Headroom nodes |
| us-west-2 | a100.80gb | 32 | 1200 | 30 | 5 |
| us-east-1 | p4d.24xlarge | 16 | 600 | 14 | 3 |

Scaling policy (template)
1. If avg queue length per node > 12 for 3 consecutive 30s windows -> scale +2 nodes.
2. If 99th latency > target for 3m -> scale +5% or move traffic to a fallback model.
3. For scale down: only when avg GPU util < 35% for 15m and queue length < 5.

Cloud accounts & networking standards
- Account model: one core infra account (shared services) + per-environment accounts (prod, staging, dev) + per-customer accounts for Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Account bootstrap: follow the account bootstrap module (Terraform) that provisions: Central logging S3, CloudWatch/Logging buckets, VPC, default IAM roles, and SSO assignments.
- VPC design: 3-tier subnets (management, compute, external). Use prefix allocation and consistent CIDR blocks per region. Document the CIDR plan in the infra-team wiki page.
- Networking patterns: use Transit Gateway (AWS) or VPC Peering only for low-bandwidth control plane paths. For Dedicated customer deployments prefer Transit Gateway or AWS PrivateLink for control plane connectivity.
- Cross-account IAM: use short-lived cross-account role assumption with AWS STS and scoped permissions following least privilege. Avoid long-lived cross-account keys.

Networking example: route table snippet (Terraform)
```hcl
resource \"aws_route\" \"to_internet\" {
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.compute.id
  destination_cidr_block = \"0.0.0.0/0\"
  gateway_id             = aws_internet_gateway.main.id
}
```

Terraform / IaC modules & best practices
- Module registry: all internal reusable modules live in the infra-modules repo. Modules must be versioned (semantic versioning) and published to the internal registry.
- Module review requirements: any change to shared modules requires: design doc PR, module bump PR, module consumers updated in canary environments, and a 48h observation period before rolling to prod.
- Backend state: remote S3 with server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) and DynamoDB locking for Terraform state. Each environment has separate state buckets and DynamoDB tables.
- Secrets management: do not store secrets in TF state. Use the secrets manager integration (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager + KMS) and reference at runtime via providers.
- Version pinning: Terraform core and provider versions must be pinned in CI. Module versions in root modules must be explicit; avoid using floating refs.

Example module usage
```hcl
module \"gpu_node_group\" {
  source = \"registry/internal/aws/gpu-node-group\"
  version = \"1.3.2\"
  instance_type = \"p4d.24xlarge\"
  desired_gpu_count = 16
  labels = { workload = \"inference\" }
}
```

CI/CD and build pipeline standards
- Pipeline structure: build -> unit tests -> integration tests (in staging infra) -> security scan -> canary deploy -> rollout. All pipeline steps are defined in the infra-pipelines repo (shared templates).
- Image builds: use immutable builds with digest pinning. Images are promoted across registries via signed SBOMs and GPG-based signing.
- Gating: PRs that change Terraform state or module versions must include plan output and be approved by at least one module owner and one infra-sre.
- Rollout strategy: use incremental canaries (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with automated rollback conditions based on latency, error rate, and pod restarts.
- CI secrets: stored in the CI provider vault and audited; ephemeral runners preferable for sensitive workloads.

Sample CI snippet (GitHub Actions style)
```yaml
name: tf-plan
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1
        with:
          terraform_version: 1.4.6
      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend-config=\"bucket=${{ secrets.TF_STATE_BUCKET }}\"
      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: terraform plan -out=tfplan
```

Runbooks and common operational playbooks
1) GPU node failure / high OOM rate - Symptoms: pod evictions, high GPU memory pressure, OOMKilled events in last 10m.
- Immediate actions:
   a. Identify affected node group: kubectl get pods -o wide | grep OOMKilled
   b. Drain node and cordon: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
   c. Scale up replacement nodes in the same instance class and attach to LB.
   d. Collect artifacts: dmesg, kubelet logs, container logs, nvidia-smi output and upload to the incident artifact S3 bucket.
   e. If issue is model-related (e.g., KV cache blowup), revert to previous model variant and open a regression ticket.

2) Autoscaler failing to scale up - Symptoms: queue length rising, pods pending with \"Insufficient GPU\"
- Immediate actions:
  1. Check autoscaler logs and metrics: (CloudWatch / Prometheus).
  2. Confirm quotas in cloud account (GPUs, vCPUs). If quota hit, escalate to cloud-ops to request quota increase.
  3. Temporarily increase headroom by moving low-priority workloads to spare region or fallback model.

3) Terraform plan shows unexpected drift / resource deletion - Actions:
  - Do not apply. Mark PR as blocked and notify module owners.
  - Run `terraform state list` and `terraform show -json` to capture current state for audit.
  - If resource must be removed, follow change management: submit change request with blast radius, rollback plan, and runbook.

Incident triage checklist
- Severity assessment, customer impact (yes/no), services affected, earliest known occurrence, mitigation steps, post-incident Go/No-Go for rollback.
- Collect metrics dump (Prometheus snapshot), logs (last 30m), and the Terraform plan for any infra changes in the last 24h.

Oncall & escalation matrix
- Pager duty routing: infra-sre -> infra-eng oncall -> oncall-manager -> eng-vp.
- For capacity-related incidents (quota, autoscaling failures) escalate to cloud-ops after 15 minutes of mitigation attempts.

Change management and release checklist
- Confirmed plan reviewed and approved by module owner and infra-sre.
- Verified canary deployment in staging for at least 2 hours with no regressions.
- Update capacity metadata spreadsheet and notify #infra-deployments channel with planned window.
- Ensure Terraform state backup snapshot is present and KMS keys are available for decryption.

Operational metrics & dashboards to maintain
- GPU pool overview: total GPUs, free GPUs, avg utilization, per-instance-class utilization.
- Region health: pod restarts, failed deployments, average scaling latency.
- CI/CD health: median pipeline duration, failure rate, average time to merge.

Appendices
A. Terraform backend example (S3 + DynamoDB)
```hcl
terraform {
  backend \"s3\" {
    bucket = \"redwood-tf-state-prod\"
    key    = \"global/infra/terraform.tfstate\"
    region = \"us-west-2\"
    dynamodb_table = \"redwood-terraform-locks\"
    encrypt = true
  }
}
```

B. Helpful CLI commands
- Check GPU utilization: kubectl -n inference exec -it <pod> -- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory --format=csv
- Find pending pods due to GPU: kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o wide | grep -i gpu
- Drain node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force

C. Owner matrix
- infra-eng: GPU fleet capacity and autoscaler development
- infra-sre: 24x7 oncall, runbooks, paging and incident management
- infra-ci: CI/CD templates, pipeline maintenance and image signing
- security: secrets management and compliance gating

Related pages and next steps
- Schedule quarterly capacity review: owners must post updates to this doc and the capacity worksheet before the review.
- For new instance classes or quantization profiles, follow the model-onboarding checklist in applied-ml-and-evals.
